opus-5.5.text:
It's a question I think about a lot, actually, because there's a strange mirroring between the two.

When I was learning mathematics, especially in competitions and later in research, a lot of my growth came from a very particular loop. You attempt a problem, you get stuck, you write something down that you *think* is a proof, and then either a mentor, a referee, or your own later self finds the gap. Over time you develop taste: a sense of which approaches are promising, which lemmas are worth proving, when an argument "smells" wrong before you can say why. That intuition isn't magic. It's compressed experience from thousands of failed attempts and corrections.

Training AI for mathematics forces you to make that loop explicit. With a human student, the feedback is fuzzy: a professor says "this step isn't convincing." With a system, you have to decide what counts as a correct step, what the reward signal is, how you verify. That's why formal verification, with proof assistants like Lean, matters so much to me. It plays the role my mentors used to play, but it never gets tired and never gets fooled by a confident-sounding argument. Honestly, it's humbling, because I've written proofs I was sure were right that a formal checker would have rejected immediately.

The other side is that working on AI has changed how I see my own thinking. You start asking: what was I actually doing when I had that insight? Was it search? Analogy? Pattern-matching against some problem I'd seen years ago? Trying to build systems that reason makes you a more careful observer of your own reasoning.

I don't see it as AI replacing the mathematician I was trying to become. It feels more like an extension of the same project. Mathematics has always been about building tools that let us see further, whether that's notation, calculus, or computers. If we can build systems that generate conjectures, check proofs, and explore spaces humans can't, the human mathematician's role shifts toward choosing what's beautiful and what's worth knowing. To me that's still the most mathematical part of the whole enterprise.

r001.rationale: The response compares learning and AI training through attempts, feedback, and correction, but does not say that problem difficulty increases as performance improves.

r002.rationale: The response mentions search as a possible part of reasoning, but does not compare observing AI use brute force with the speaker’s experience as a mathematician.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it as two versions of the same question, actually. When I was learning mathematics, the thing that mattered most wasn't how many theorems I had memorized. It was the moments when I got stuck on a problem for days, tried an approach, watched it fail, and had to figure out why it failed before I could try something else. That loop of attempt, failure, and reflection is where the real learning happened. And it's exactly the loop that's hardest to give to a model.

Most of what's written down in mathematics is the finished product. Papers show the clean proof. Textbooks show the polished argument. Nobody publishes the forty pages of scratch work where they went down the wrong path and came back. So when you train on text alone, the model sees the answers but almost never sees the thinking. That's a bit like trying to become a mathematician by only reading the last page of every proof.

So a lot of what we're doing is trying to reconstruct that missing process. Let the model attempt a problem, verify whether the reasoning actually holds, feed that signal back. Formal verification helps here because it gives you a ground truth that doesn't lie to you. In my own training as a mathematician, my advisor was that verifier. She would look at my argument and say, this step doesn't follow. For a model, we need something that can play that role at scale.

The other thing I keep coming back to is taste. Good mathematicians don't just prove things, they know which problems are worth attacking and which lemmas are likely to be true before they've proved them. I developed that slowly, by being around people who had it and absorbing how they thought. I don't think we fully understand how to instill that in a model yet, and honestly that's the part I find most interesting. If we can figure out what taste is in a way concrete enough to train on, I think we'll understand something about how humans learn mathematics too.

astra-6.text:
I see a parallel in the way feedback shapes learning. As a mathematician, you try an approach, discover where it breaks, and gradually develop a better sense of which ideas are worth pursuing. The failed attempts are part of how you build intuition.

That also shapes how I think about training AI. Getting the right answer matters, but I’m interested in whether a system can recognize a mistake, revise its approach, and carry what it learned into a different problem. In mathematics, that’s a much stronger sign of understanding than reproducing a solution you’ve already seen.

And the connection goes both ways. Thinking about how to train an AI makes me ask what actually helped me learn: when I needed an example, when I needed feedback, and when I needed time to struggle with a problem myself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an interesting parallel: in both cases, you’re asking what it means to learn something deeply rather than just reproduce an answer. As a mathematician, I can read a proof and follow every line, but that doesn’t necessarily mean I could have discovered it myself. The real test is whether I can use those ideas when I encounter a new problem.

That’s also how I think about training AI. Getting the right answer is valuable, but I’m interested in whether the system has learned something that transfers. Can it recognize a useful structure in an unfamiliar setting? Can it recover when its first approach fails?

And that perspective feeds back into my own development. It makes me ask whether I’m building understanding or just getting comfortable with familiar techniques. Sometimes struggling with a problem is precisely what helps me see the distinction.
